It describes ordinary acts of violence: soldiers strike Jesus (Mark 15:19, Matthew 27:30), an unfaithful servant strikes his companions (Matthew 24:49, Luke 12:45), Sosthenes is beaten before the tribunal (Acts 18:17), or Paul is struck on the mouth (Acts 23:2). It can also denote an expressive act: the crowd striking their chests as a sign of grief (Luke 23:48, Luke 18:13). In contexts of court or violence, the verb is almost neutral, simply reporting the action. But when it comes to self-flagellation of repentance or grief, it takes on an emotional nuance. Metaphorically, it describes the action of God who "strikes" with punishment (Acts 23:3), drawing from the Old Testament, or one who "wounds" a brother's conscience (1 Corinthians 8:12).
G5180.portee: This word reminds us how Jesus endured blows and physical humiliation without retaliating, fulfilling Scripture. It invites the reader to recognize their own inner violence — mistreatment, malice, contempt for others — and to seek heart transformation. The image of repentance striking the chest also shows that true conversion hides nothing: it confesses before God with unreserved sincerity.

sens: Name of a person, schoolmaster in Ephesus
G5181.detail: Tyrannus is the name of a man who owned a school in Ephesus, an important city in Asia Minor. It was in this school that the apostle Paul taught the Gospel after having to leave the synagogue, where some resisted his message (Acts 19:9).
G5181.origine: The name Tyrannus comes from ancient Greek and would originally mean "absolute master" or "sovereign." It is related to Greek words denoting authority (such as κύριος, lord). Although it is a common personal name in the Greek world, it carries the idea of a certain authority or mastery — fitting for a schoolmaster.
G5181.emploi: Tyrannus is mentioned only once in the New Testament, in Acts 19:9, where he is presented as the owner of a school in Ephesus. This man and his school play a significant practical role in Paul's mission: it is there that the apostle was able to teach daily for about two years (see Acts 19:10), making Jesus and the Gospel known to all who came to listen. The mention of Tyrannus illustrates how God used ordinary circumstances and secondary characters to advance His plan of salvation.

sens: inhabitant or native of Tyre
G5183.detail: The Tyrians are the inhabitants of the city of Tyre, a major Phoenician port on the current Mediterranean coast of Lebanon. In the passage of Acts 12:20, it is delegates from this city who come to seek peace with King Herod, as their country depended economically on the king's kingdom for food supplies.
G5183.origine: The Greek word Turios ("Tyrian") comes directly from the name of the city of Tyre, a major commercial and maritime center of antiquity. Tyre means "rock" in Phoenician, which evokes its geographical situation on a rocky island and then a peninsula. The name is simply formed by adding the Greek ending that indicates origin or belonging to the name of the city.
G5183.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 12:20. It designates the representatives of the city of Tyre who present themselves before King Herod to negotiate. The context shows the political and economic importance of Tyre: its inhabitants needed the commercial support of Herod's kingdom to feed their population.
G5183.portee: This passage reminds us that coastal cities like Tyre, despite their wealth and commercial power, remained dependent on their neighbors for essential resources. It illustrates the interdependence of nations and the fragility of political relations at the time of the New Testament.

sens: Port city of Phoenicia, located on the Mediterranean coast
Prosperous commercial and maritime center
Region or territory surrounding the city
G5184.detail:
1. Tyre is a large port city of ancient Phoenicia (modern-day Lebanon), established on the Mediterranean coast. It was one of the most important cities of this eastern world, known for its maritime trade and wealth. Jesus mentions it as an example of a city that, although foreign to Israel, would have responded better to His miracles than some cities of Israel: "If the miracles that were performed in your midst had been performed in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago" (Matthew 11:21).
2. The territory or region around Tyre is also designated by this word. Jesus "withdrew to the region of Tyre and Sidon" (Matthew 15:21) and crowds from "the vicinity of Tyre and Sidon" pressed around Him (Mark 3:8).
G5184.origine: Tyre is an ancient Phoenician name that literally means "rock." The city was indeed built on a fortified rocky island and peninsula, which explains why it was such a powerful commercial and military center. The Greek name Τύρος directly reflects the Semitic name of the city.
G5184.emploi: Tyre appears 11 times in the New Testament, mainly in Matthew, Mark, and Luke, often in parallel with Sidon, its neighbor. Jesus cites it as an example of a pagan city that would have listened to the Gospel better than Chorazin and Bethsaida, Jewish cities (Matthew 11:21-22 and Luke 10:13-14). It is also mentioned as a destination or region traversed by Jesus during His travels in Galilee (Mark 7:24-31, Matthew 15:21), and finally as a port where Paul stops during his journey to Jerusalem (Acts 21:3, 7).
G5184.portee: Tyre illustrates that Jesus does not limit His reach to Israel alone: even the pagan cities of the Phoenician coast are included in His message and would be capable of faith. The example of Tyre also teaches the urgency of repentance: a city famous for its commercial and political power would have renounced all of that in the face of clear signs of God's action. This challenges the reader regarding the true value of repentance before the works of God.

sens: Unable to see, deprived of sight
Lacking clarity of vision, lacking discernment
Acting without reflection, ignoring the consequences
G5185.detail:
1. The blind person is one who has lost or never had the ability to see. This is a very real physical infirmity in the Gospels: Jesus spits on the ground and applies mud to the eyes of the blind man from Bethsaida to heal him (Mark 8:22). Blindness was a common affliction in Palestine, and the blind are often mentioned alongside the lame, lepers, and other sick individuals.
2. In a figurative sense, the blind person is one who does not see spiritually — who does not understand the truth of God. Jesus asks his disciples: "Can a blind man lead a blind man?" (Luke 6:39), showing the absurdity of someone claiming to teach without seeing the reality themselves. The Pharisees are called "blind" because they do not recognize that Jesus is the Messiah (Matthew 23:16-26).
3. This spiritual blindness is a voluntary ignorance: it arises from the refusal to see the light offered. Jesus says: "I came that the blind may see" (John 9:39), for his coming brings clarity. Those who refuse this light remain in darkness.
G5185.origine: The Greek word τυφλός comes from a root that evokes darkness and the absence of light. In Hebrew, עִוֵּר (ivér) also designates one who does not see. This image of blindness as deprivation of light is profound: to see is to be in contact with reality; to be blind is to be separated from it. The Bible often uses the light-darkness pair to express knowledge of God and spiritual ignorance.
G5185.emploi: The word "blind" appears 47 times in the New Testament, primarily in the Gospels. Matthew and Luke recount several healings of blind people by Jesus (Matthew 9:27; 20:30; Luke 7:22), showing that Jesus has the power to restore sight — a messianic sign expected by Israel. John 9 dedicates an entire chapter to a man born blind, a story that contrasts physical healing with the spiritual blindness of the Pharisees who refuse to believe. The figurative sense dominates elsewhere: Matthew 23:16-26 accumulates the reproach of "blind" against the Pharisees and scribes, while Romans 2:19 and 2 Peter 1:9 address Christians who risk going astray spiritually. In Revelation 3:17, Jesus tells the Church of Laodicea that it believes it is rich but is "blind" — it is unaware of its true condition.
G5185.portee: For the Christian, this word challenges on two levels. First, it reminds us that Jesus came to bring light to those in darkness — the physical blindness that Jesus heals symbolizes the spiritual blindness from which he frees us. Secondly, it warns us: spiritual blindness is a real danger, less visible than physical blindness but more serious, as it deprives us of seeing God himself. The Christian must examine their heart to ensure they have not closed their eyes to the truth.

sens: To make blind, to take away sight
To prevent from seeing, understanding a truth
To obscure spiritual understanding
G5186.detail:
1. In the literal sense: to make someone blind, to take away their ability to see physically. The Greek word τυφλόω comes from the adjective τυφλός (blind) and denotes this action of depriving of sight.
2. In a figurative sense: to prevent someone from perceiving or understanding something evident. In 2 Corinthians 4:4, the god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers, meaning he has prevented them from seeing the glory of the Gospel shine, as if a veil covered their understanding.
3. Spiritually: to cause moral and spiritual blindness. In 1 John 2:11, hatred toward a brother blinds the eyes of the heart, causing one to walk in darkness without knowing where they are going. In John 12:40, God has blinded the eyes of the Israelites so that they do not see or understand, for fear that they might turn — which evokes divine judgment on those who reject the light.
G5186.origine: The verb τυφλόω derives from the Greek adjective τυφλός (blind, deprived of sight). The starting image is that of the physical deprivation of light and vision. In Hebrew from the Old Testament, the word עִוֵּר ("blind") carries the same concrete meaning. The Bible often uses blindness, whether physical or moral, as an image of ignorance and refusal of divine truth.
G5186.emploi: The verb τυφλόω appears only three times in the New Testament. In John 12:40, it reports a divine judgment: God blinds the eyes of those who refuse to believe, a quotation from the Old Testament (Isaiah 6:10). In 2 Corinthians 4:4, Paul describes how the god of this age blinds the minds of unbelievers to prevent them from seeing the Gospel — here, the word expresses the work of lies and spiritual deception in the face of truth. In 1 John 2:11, brotherly hatred produces moral blindness: whoever hates their brother no longer sees clearly in the darkness where they walk. In all cases, to blind is never a simple physical loss, but a spiritual obstruction.
G5186.portee: This word reminds us that the truth of the Gospel can be hidden from those who lock themselves in unbelief, deception, or hatred. It exhorts us to watch over our hearts: hatred can plunge us into darkness, taking away our ability to see God. It also shows us that only the light of Christ can open the closed eyes of spiritual ignorance.

sens: To be inflated with smoke that obscures judgment
To be puffed up with pride and vanity
To lose reason under the influence of self-importance
To become arrogant and contemptuous
G5187.detail:
1. The word comes from a very concrete image: that of smoke that envelops and blinds. It is a swelling that blurs vision, preventing clear sight. In 1 Timothy 3:6, the new convert risks being "puffed up with pride" — literally swollen as if by smoke — and thus falling under the judgment of the devil.
2. This pride is not a simple minor fault: it is a state that makes someone vain and self-sufficient. In 1 Timothy 6:4, the one who "is puffed up with pride" "knows nothing" — their swelling blinds them to their own ignorance, leading them to sterile disputes and quarrels about words.
3. This self-sufficiency creates a separation from reality and from God. In 2 Timothy 3:4, those who are "puffed up with pride" love "pleasure more than God": their heart has no room for the true.
4. The word denotes less an aggressive anger than a form of selfishness that is unaware of itself: one is inflated with their own importance and does not even see it. It is a moral and spiritual blindness.
G5187.origine: The word comes from τῦφος (tuphós), which literally means smoke or fog — this vapor that rises and veils. By extension, the word has taken on a figurative meaning: vanity, arrogance, anything that "goes to one's head" and obscures judgment. The verb is found in the writings of Greek authors (Demosthenes, Aristotle) with the same metaphorical meaning. It is a very expressive word: it paints pride as a kind of smoke that fills someone with themselves.
G5187.emploi: The verb appears only three times in the New Testament, and always in the passive voice ("to be puffed up"), which emphasizes that it is something that happens to someone, a condition into which they fall. The three occurrences are in the letters to Timothy, which address the moral qualities a Christian leader must have and the spiritual dangers threatening the Church. In 1 Timothy 3:6, it is a warning: a young believer who becomes prideful becomes vulnerable to God's judgment. In 1 Timothy 6:4 and 2 Timothy 3:4, pride is associated with other vices — pretentious ignorance, love of pleasure, betrayal — showing that this "swelling" destroys spiritual and moral life.
G5187.portee: This word warns us that pride is not a simple attitude fault: it is a spiritual blindness that separates us from God and from the truth. It rises to the head like smoke that obscures the sky. For a new believer especially, vigilance is necessary: successes or gifts received can inflate the heart without one noticing. Biblical wisdom consists of remaining humble, aware of our ignorance and weakness, to keep a heart open to God.

sens: To emit smoke, produce a light smoke
To burn slowly while smoking, to burn faintly
Figuratively, to persist weakly, to survive despite everything
G5188.detail:
1. The verb describes the action of producing smoke. In Matthew 12:20, it refers to a wick or a dimly burning lamp that smokes — a small flame that is consumed while emitting smoke, like a poorly burning candle.

2. The underlying image is that of weak, incomplete combustion: the fire does not consume all at once, it smolders. The lamp does not shine brightly, it smokes; it is a flickering, almost dying light, but it still persists.

3. Applied to situations or people, the word evokes a lingering weakness: something that is not extinguished, that does not completely disappear, even if it is reduced to very little. In Matthew 12:20, the messianic context gives the verb a spiritual significance: Christ does not eliminate what is weak or damaged, but rather supports it until its complete restoration.
G5188.origine: The verb comes from the noun τῦφος (tuphós), which means "smoke." It literally describes the action of producing smoke. The root evokes the idea of mist, vapor — something that rises but remains ephemeral. The word belongs to a Greek family related to smoke and to what obscures or is insubstantial.
G5188.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 12:20. Matthew cites it to describe the behavior of the announced Messiah: a lamp that smokes — a metaphor for the weak, the damaged, the one who barely survives. The citation comes from the Old Testament (Isaiah 42:3), where it announces a Servant who does not break the bruised reed and does not extinguish the smoking wick. The meaning remains constant: an image of gentleness, respect for fragility and lack.
G5188.portee: This word invites the reader to see how Jesus, the Messiah, treats weary and broken souls: not by rejecting or finishing them off, but by preserving them, supporting them, until they regain their strength. It is a word of comfort for all those who feel reduced to almost nothing, consumed by suffering, holding on by a thread. It affirms Christ's tenderness towards the weak.

sens: Of a wild and irresistible violence, manifested brutally
Acting or moving with unrestrained, unleashed force
G5189.detail:
1. The word describes a natural phenomenon of extreme violence: a wind, a storm that suddenly arises and ravages everything in its path. In Acts 27:14, it is the wind Euroclydon that "breaks loose upon the island" with unpredictable brutality — the adjective captures this unleashed fury of nature.
2. Figuratively, it qualifies any force or movement characterized by overflowing, uncontrollable energy, charging straight ahead without restraint.
G5189.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek "typhon" (τῦφος), which means "smoke" or "fog," and also refers to the swirling wind, the storm, or in mythology, the giant Typhon, the embodiment of the storm. The adjective "impetuous" takes up this idea: a force that unfolds with the chaotic violence of a tornado or cyclone, irrepressible and wild.
G5189.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:14, where Luke reports the storm that nearly shipwrecked Paul's vessel sailing to Rome. The context is dramatic: a wind called Euroclydon (a feared northeast wind among sailors) suddenly arises and sweeps the ship away. The adjective "impetuous" emphasizes the devastating and unexpected nature of this violent gust.
G5189.portee: This word reminds Christians of the reality of the storms that assail life — crises, trials, events that seem to escape us. But Acts 27 also shows that even in the midst of such violence, God does not abandon us: Paul and all the travelers are saved. The impetuosity of the wind does not equal the faithfulness of God.

sens: Traveling companion of the Apostle Paul
G5190.detail: Tychicus is a man who accompanied Paul during his missionary journeys. In Acts 20:4, he is among those who escorted Paul to Asia, alongside Sopater, Aristarchus, and other faithful ones. Later, Paul sends him as a trusted messenger to the churches: he is sent to the Ephesians to inform them of Paul's condition in prison (Ephesians 6:21), and likewise to the Colossians to communicate the news (Colossians 4:7). Paul refers to him as a "beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord," which shows his esteem for him. At the end of his life, Paul sends him to Ephesus (2 Timothy 4:12) and considers sending him or Artemas to Titus so that Titus can come to him (Titus 3:12). Tychicus thus embodies the role of the faithful collaborator who connects the apostle to the churches.
G5190.origine: The name Tychicus comes from ancient Greek and literally means "linked to fortune" or "lucky," from the word τύχη (tychè) which denotes chance or luck. Although etymologically related to this secular notion, the name was borne by this faithful disciple who was, spiritually, much more than a matter of chance: a deliberate blessing for the churches he served.
G5190.emploi: Tychicus appears seven times in the New Testament, exclusively in the later Pauline epistles (Acts, Ephesians, Colossians, 2 Timothy, Titus). He is first mentioned in Acts 20:4 as one of Paul's companions who traveled with him. Then, in the captivity epistles (Ephesians and Colossians), he is presented as the bearer of the letters Paul addresses to the churches, a very important mediating role: he must not only convey the text but also complete the explanations verbally. In later epistles (2 Timothy and Titus), he is mentioned as someone Paul can send or circulate according to the needs of the ministry. Everywhere, he is designated by honorific titles ("beloved brother," "faithful minister"), showing that Paul fully trusted him.
G5190.portee: Tychicus illustrates the essential role of unknown but faithful collaborators in the expansion of the early Church. He is not an apostle, but a minister of Christ entirely at the service of proclaiming the Gospel and providing pastoral support to the churches. His existence reminds the reader that the Christian life does not require being a "great" person to be a valuable instrument of God: it is faithfulness in daily service that matters. Tychicus also shows us how the apostolic Church was a communion of saints who mutually supported each other and communicated Paul's exhortations.

sens: A dark blue or intense blue-violet
A shade reminiscent of the hyacinth stone or flower
G5191.detail:
1. The word describes a specific color: a deep blue, almost violet, reminiscent of the hyacinth flower. In Revelation 9:17, the breastplates of the horsemen in the vision have this intense dark blue hue, mixed with colors of fire and sulfur. It is a color that is both rich and dark, evoking something impressive and formidable.

2. The word can also refer to the blue-violet hue that sulfurous smoke or flames take on when they burn intensely. This shade of blue in a context of fire and sulfur reinforces the supernatural and terrifying aspect of the apocalyptic vision: colors that are not natural, blending the blue of the sky or precious stone with the chaos of divine judgment.
G5191.origine: The word comes from the name of the hyacinth flower (ὑάκινθος in Greek). This flower, known in the ancient Mediterranean world, typically had a characteristic blue-violet color. The adjective "color of hyacinth" naturally formed to describe anything that had this distinctive hue. In Hebrew, the Old Testament uses words like תְּכֵלֶת (blue, notably the blue of royal purple) for similar shades.
G5191.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Revelation 9:17. John describes a symbolic vision: horses with breastplates and ridden by horsemen whose armors have three different colors — fire, hyacinth, and sulfur. This enumeration creates a dark and threatening visual impression, blending deep blue with shades of destruction. The color of hyacinth here does not speak of natural beauty but of a terrifying vision, that of divine judgment approaching.
G5191.portee: This word reminds us that in Revelation, John uses precise images and often colors to make palpable what is supernatural and would otherwise escape our understanding. The color of hyacinth is not chosen at random: it makes visible the judgment of God, which descends with power and majesty. For the reader, this reinforces the real and frightening nature of this prophetic vision.

sens: Precious stone of dark blue color, used to adorn the heavenly Jerusalem
Blue or violet flower (classical usage)
G5192.detail:
1. In Revelation, the hyacinth is a precious stone of deep blue that is among the twelve stones forming the foundations of the heavenly Jerusalem (Revelation 21:20). John names it as the eleventh of the twelve minerals that adorn the holy wall, thus signaling its great value and beauty. It is a precious stone, probably what we call sapphire or a variety of blue coral.
2. In classical Greek literature, the word originally referred to a flower, presumably the dark blue iris or another flower of violet hue. Over time, the same word was applied to a gemstone of similar color, thus creating a link between the natural beauty of the flower and the luster of the polished mineral.
G5192.origine: The Greek word "hyakinthos" comes from Greek mythology: according to ancient legends, it referred to a flower created from the blood of a beloved young man, transformed by the gods. The Hebrew word תְּכֵלֶת (tekheleth), usually translated as "blue" or "purple-blue" in the Septuagint, is often rendered by this term to express the same idea of a luxurious dark blue shade. The family of the word extends to various words denoting colors and stones in ancient languages.
G5192.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 21:20, in John's vision describing the foundations of the New Jerusalem. In this solemn eschatological context, John enumerates twelve precious stones, each representing exceptional beauty and value, adorning the wall of the celestial city. The use here is highly symbolic: each stone recalls the glory, purity, and eternity of the kingdom of God. The deep blue of the hyacinth evokes the divine sky and transcendence.
G5192.portee: The hyacinth, mentioned in the vision of the new heaven, reminds the believer that future glory is not immaterial or vague, but adorned with concrete and radiant beauty. This stone encourages contemplation of the splendor that God prepares for His own, beyond what our eyes see today. It invites us to place our hope in the glorious and tangible reality of the eternal kingdom.

sens: Made of glass, transparent and smooth like glass
Shining with a crystalline and pure luster
G5193.detail: 1. The word designates what is made of glass or has its appearance: a transparent, hard, and smooth material. In John's vision, the "sea of glass" (Revelation 4:6) evokes a vast, flat, and shining surface, similar to polished glass — an image of purity and clarity before the throne of God. 2. The adjective also emphasizes brilliance and transparency: the "sea of glass, mingled with fire" (Revelation 15:2) shines with a heavenly light that suggests divine glory and the victory of the redeemed. Glass, rare and precious in antiquity, symbolizes here something beautiful, pure, and celestial.
G5193.origine: The Greek word comes from ὕαλος (hualos), which means "glass." This name designates both the material and the finished object (vase, window). The basic image is that of a transparent and shining substance, different from natural crystal but equally admired. The word is specifically used in Revelation to describe celestial realities.
G5193.emploi: The adjective "of glass" appears twice in Revelation, in chapters 4 and 15, always to qualify a vast expanse of supernatural water. In Revelation 4:6, it appears as an element of the divine throne, of crystalline purity. In Revelation 15:2, it symbolizes the victory of Christians who have triumphed over the beast: standing on this glorious sea, they celebrate God. The context is always liturgical and eschatological — the vision of eternal realities and the glory of God.
G5193.portee: This word invites the reader to contemplate the beauty and purity of the divine presence. The "sea of glass" is neither threatening nor opaque: it is translucent, inviting one to see beyond. For the believer, it symbolizes that the final victory is not dark or distant, but radiant and accessible — a reality where the redeemed will stand in the light of God.

sens: Transparent and clear stone
Vitreous material, shiny and translucent, shaped by man
G5194.detail: 1. The word primarily designates a clear and transparent natural stone, probably crystal or a shiny semi-precious stone: this is the ancient meaning of the word in Greek. 2. From classical times, it applies to glass, this shiny and transparent material that is manufactured. In Revelation, John sees the place of the celestial city as "transparent glass" (Revelation 21:21): it evokes a crystalline perfection, smooth and clear, that reflects light without disturbing it. It is an image of absolute purity.
G5194.origine: The Greek word ὕαλος comes from an ancient Indo-European root denoting clarity and transparency. In Hebrew, the Bible uses זְכוּכִית (zekhokkhit) for glass, a word that is related to a family expressing purity and brilliance. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, this Hebrew word is often rendered by ὕαλος.
G5194.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Revelation chapter 21, in the description of the heavenly Jerusalem. John first describes "pure gold, like clear glass" for the wall (Revelation 21:18), then "the place of the city was pure gold, like transparent glass" (Revelation 21:21). In both cases, glass symbolizes transparency, absolute clarity, and immaculate purity of the eternal city, in contrast to the opacity of the earthly world.
G5194.portee: This word invites the Christian to contemplate the perfection and transparency of communion with God in heaven. Clear glass evokes the idea that in the heavenly Jerusalem, nothing will be hidden, everything will be clear and luminous. It is a promise of total clarity: we will see face to face, without veil.

sens: To treat someone with contempt and violence, to humiliate them through offensive words or actions
To insult or slander someone
To commit violence against someone, to mistreat or injure them
To show insolent contempt towards a person
G5195.detail:
1. To outrage is to treat someone brutally and contemptuously, intentionally to reduce them to humiliation. In the parable of Matthew 22:6, the king sends his servants to deliver a message, but these messengers are "outraged": they are not only refused; they are insulted and harmed. It is both a verbal and physical act, motivated by contempt.
2. The word emphasizes the insult and the hurtful words, the slander directed at someone to dishonor them. When Jesus accuses the Pharisees of saying too much, in Luke 11:45, a lawyer protests: "You also outrage us" — that is, you insult us, you treat us indignantly with your words.
3. To outrage can also mean to commit violence against someone, to injure or mistreat them physically. In Luke 18:32, it is announced that Jesus "will be outraged" by the Gentiles: this includes mockery, spitting, blows — total violence inflicted to humiliate him.
4. It is always an act of insolence: the one who outrages despises their opponent and wants to publicly belittle them, treating them as unworthy of respect. In 1 Thessalonians 2:2, Paul reminds that after suffering "outrages" in Philippi (arrest, mistreatment in prison), the Gospel was not stifled.
G5195.origine: The word comes from the Greek root ὕβρις (hubris), which primarily means excess, arrogance, insolence — this attitude of one who believes they are above all. To outrage is to act under the influence of this hubris, that is, to manifest violent and arrogant contempt towards someone. In Greek tradition, hubris is the supreme sin, that of the man who forgets the limits and insults the gods or his fellow beings. The Bible adopts this concept to describe insolent contempt and mistreatment.
G5195.emploi: The verb appears 5 times in the New Testament, always to describe a hostile action towards people. It is mainly found in the Gospels and Acts, recounting how the adversaries of Jesus and the apostles treat them with violence and disdain. In Matthew 22:6 and Acts 14:5, it is the people or the Gentiles who "outrage" the messengers or the apostles. In Luke 11:45 and Luke 18:32, it is the insult or mistreatment inflicted on Jesus himself. In 1 Thessalonians 2:2, Paul uses the derived noun (outrages) to qualify the sufferings and humiliations he endured, but without allowing these blows to crush his courage. The word always describes a gesture of deliberate hostility, never a simple disagreement.
G5195.portee: To outrage reminds us that malice towards God's messengers or towards Jesus himself is a serious act of contempt, not a mere disagreement. For the Christian, it is also a word of comfort: Jesus suffered outrage (Luke 18:32), and the apostles endured it (1 Thessalonians 2:2); their reproaches do not come from a failure of God, but from a hostile heart that rejects his message. Finally, this word warns us: to treat with insolence and contempt those who speak of God is to fall into arrogance and the sin of hubris.

sens: Violence, insult, or mistreatment inflicted deliberately on someone
Serious peril or danger, especially for a ship at sea
Arrogance, insolence, haughty contempt for the established order
G5196.detail:
1. Outrage is primarily an act of deliberate violence: hitting, insulting, humiliating someone to dominate or despise them. In 2 Corinthians 12:10, Paul lists the "outrages" he has suffered for Christ — mockery, blows, intentional humiliations meant to belittle him.
2. The word also denotes a great peril or serious damage. In Acts 27:10 and 27:21, Paul warns the travelers that continuing navigation at the wrong time will cause "peril" — he speaks of the risk of storm and shipwreck threatening the vessel. The danger comes from disregarding the weather conditions: one ignores the warning and rushes headlong.
3. At its root, the word expresses insolence: the attitude of one who breaks the rules, who insults the natural or moral order through pride and arrogance. That is why the Bible associates this outrage with contempt and rebellion.
G5196.origine: The Greek word hubris comes from a root expressing excess, arrogance. In Hebrew, it mainly translates "gaʾôn" (גָּאוֹן), which denotes haughty pride and arrogance. The family of the word includes verbal and nominal forms related to contempt and insolent violence. It is a classical term in Greek morality, which sees hubris as the supreme sin — one that drives a person to violate divine or natural order and attracts the vengeance of the gods.
G5196.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, always in Paul. Two occurrences are found in Acts 27, where Paul describes maritime peril: he uses "hubris" to express the growing danger of traveling in bad weather — this danger arises from a violation of natural prudence, like a form of outrage against the laws of navigation. A major occurrence is found in 2 Corinthians 12:10: Paul states that he "takes pleasure" in the outrages suffered for Christ. There, the word denotes the mistreatments, blows, and humiliations inflicted on him by his adversaries. Paul presents them not as a defeat, but as an opportunity to show that the power of Christ is manifested in human weakness.
G5196.portee: Outrage reminds the reader that the true strength of the Christian does not lie in arrogance or contempt for others, but in the humble acceptance of suffering for Christ. When Paul "takes pleasure" in the outrages, he invites the believer to see in each humiliation an opportunity to manifest God's grace. Moreover, the word calls for respect for the established order: despising wisdom (like ignoring Paul's warning about maritime danger) attracts serious consequences. It is a call to prudence and the fear of God.

sens: One who allows themselves to dominate or mistreat others without respect or restraint
One who shows arrogant pride and contempt towards others
One who acts with brutal insolence
G5197.detail:
1. A violent and insolent man is someone who pushes the limits of respect and decency: he mistreats his neighbor without fear of consequence, driven by a raw desire for domination. This is the type of man Paul describes in Romans 1:30, among those who "take pleasure in doing evil."

2. It is also a character of aggressive pride: one who believes themselves superior and shows it through wicked acts or disdainful words. Paul himself admits in 1 Timothy 1:13 that he was once "violent," acting as an unrestrained persecutor.

3. Brutal insolence marks one who shamelessly crosses the line between firmness and cruelty, between confidence and contempt. It is an attitude of one who ignores or tramples on the dignity of others.
G5197.origine: The word comes from the verb "hyrizo" (to outrage), which evokes an action that exceeds all limits of decency. The root expresses the idea of crossing a boundary, of exceeding what is proper. In Hebrew, similar notions are often found such as "gueah" (haughty pride) or "azaz" (to act with arrogance). The Greek word emphasizes the active and violent aspect of this transgression: it is not just internal pride, but an arrogance that externalizes itself through acts of malice.
G5197.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Romans 1:30, Paul uses it to describe one of the characteristic traits of humanity fallen under God's judgment, in a list of vices that reflect a heart hardened to God. In 1 Timothy 1:13, Paul applies it to himself when he was a persecutor, before his conversion, highlighting the extremity of his former guilt. These two uses show a man acting with arrogant brutality, either because his heart has hardened in sin, or because he pursues a false cause with relentless zeal.
G5197.portee: This word reminds us that violence and arrogance towards others reveal a heart separated from God and blind to its own weakness. But by showing that Paul himself had been such, the Bible teaches us that even the most violent of sinners can receive mercy and be transformed. It is an invitation to recognize this tendency within us and turn towards God's grace.

sens: To enjoy good physical health, to be healed from illness
To be sound of mind, mentally solid
To be correct, accurate, without error (referring to a doctrine or teaching)
To be intact, preserved from evil or corruption
G5198.detail:
1. To be in good physical health: this is the state of one whose body functions well, who is not sick. Jesus says that those who are well do not need a physician (Luke 5:31); the servant of the prodigal son rejoices that his brother has returned in good health (Luke 15:27).
2. To be sound of mind: this is a moral and spiritual solidity, the absence of confusion or disturbance in judgment and thoughts.
3. To be correct and reliable in teaching: a doctrine or words are "sound" when they are true, faithful, and beneficial for faith. Paul calls the words of Jesus Christ "sound words" (1 Timothy 6:3) and "sound doctrine" that which should be taught (2 Timothy 4:3). It is like food that truly nourishes, as opposed to lies that poison.
4. To be intact, preserved: a sound faith, a sound charity are qualities that are uncorrupted, retaining all their virtue.
G5198.origine: The word comes from the Greek hugiès (ὑγιής), "healthy," which suggests the idea of harmony and balance of the body or soul. In Hebrew, the Septuagint often translates the word shalom (שָׁלוֹם) with this word, which means peace, wholeness, prosperity. That is why "health" and "wholeness" are closely related in this vocabulary: to be healthy is to be whole, not fragmented, not corrupted.
G5198.emploi: This verb appears twelve times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and the pastoral epistles (letters to Timothy and Titus). In the Gospels (Luke), it denotes the physical state of health: Jesus heals a centurion's servant (Luke 7:10). But in the pastoral epistles, it takes on a spiritual and doctrinal significance: Paul uses it to qualify true faith (Titus 1:13, 2:2), authentic charity, and faithful teaching. The "sound words" or "sound doctrine" oppose false doctrines that disturb the Church. This shift from physical meaning to moral meaning is typical of Paul: the health of the body becomes the image of the solidity of faith.
G5198.portee: This word reminds the Christian that faith is not vague or unstable, but a solid edifice, founded on truth. False doctrines are like a spiritual illness: they corrupt and weaken. The apostle calls us to cultivate a "sound" faith, that is, integral, coherent, rooted in the word of the Lord. It is also an invitation to discern between true spiritual food and seductive lies.

sens: Who has recovered health, who is no longer sick
Whose body functions normally, without illness or infirmity
In a figurative sense: just, sound, free from error (referring to a word or doctrine)
G5199.detail:
1. Healed means that a person has been freed from their illness or infirmity. Jesus asks the invalid at Bethsaida: "Do you want to be healed?" (John 5:6), and the man who has recovered health confides: "The one who healed me said to me: Take up your bed and walk" (John 5:11). It is the state of one who moves from illness to health.
2. Sound describes someone whose body is whole and functional, without defect or weakness. When Jesus heals the withered hand of the man, "it became sound like the other" (Matthew 12:13): the hand regains its integrity and ability to act. Mark 3:5 and Luke 6:10 report the same miracle with the same result: "his hand was healed."
3. In a figurative sense, sound qualifies a word or doctrine that is correct, in accordance with the truth. Paul urges to hold "sound speech" (Titus 2:8), that is, true and solid words, free from error.
G5199.origine: The word comes from a root that means to be whole, intact. It is related to the idea of completeness and absence of fracture or defect. In classical Greek, it denotes what is complete, without damage. The same root appears in words that evoke solidity and integrity. It is a common word to express good physical health or, by extension, moral and doctrinal correctness.
G5199.emploi: This word is used about 14 times in the New Testament, mainly in Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John, where it describes the miraculous healings of Jesus. It frequently appears in the account of the healing of the invalid at Bethsaida (John 5), marking the transition from illness to health. Mark and Luke use it for the healing of the withered hand. In Acts 4:10, Peter uses it in announcing the healing of the lame man in the name of Jesus. Finally, in Titus 2:8, Paul applies the word to speech or doctrine to signify that it is sound, right, free from falsehood. The word thus always retains the idea of transition to integrity, whether physical or moral.
G5199.portee: This word reminds us that physical healing is a sign of Jesus' power and compassion toward those who suffer. For the Christian reader, it illustrates that Jesus restores the whole person. In a figurative sense, the term also invites us to seek solid words and faith, untainted by error or lies.
